### Motivation / Background

This Pull Request has been created because apps can't choose which static files Rails serves pre-compressed.

`ActionDispatch::FileHandler` only serves a `.br`/`.gz` copy when the file's content type matches `compressible_content_types:` (text, JavaScript, SVG). The option already exists, but `ActionDispatch::Static` doesn't pass it through and there is no config setting for it. Pre-compressed JSON, WebAssembly, and other assets are always served uncompressed.

### Detail

This Pull Request changes:

- `ActionDispatch::Static` passes extra options through to `FileHandler`.
- Adds:
  - `config.public_file_server.compressible_content_types`
    - accepts an Array of content types, as well as a Regexp.
  - `config.public_file_server.precompressed`.
- Defaults are unchanged; unset settings aren't passed.

### Additional information

`compressible_content_types` replaces the default, so apps can both add and remove types.

Rough cost per request (mac m5 ssd, Ruby 3.4, benchmark-ips):

- Matching the content type: under 0.1 µs. A flat list and a hand-tuned `Regexp` differ by tens of nanoseconds.
- Checking whether a file exists: about 1 µs when it's missing, more when it exists.
- Serving a static file through `ActionDispatch::Static`: about 25–30 µs.
- Expecting linux to be quicker

So the content type check is noise; the file lookups are what cost. A compressible type with no precompressed copy adds two missing-file checks (`.br`, `.gz`). Requests that aren't files pay the most: `GET /users` has no extension, so it is checked as `text/plain` and then `text/html`, and with the default that is 9 file checks (`/users.br`, `/users.gz`, `/users`, `/users.html.br`, …) before the request reaches the app. With `text/` left out, it is 3.

Fixes #58940

Since #57695, `ActionCable::SubscriptionAdapter::Redis::Listener#reset` keeps
`@subscribe_callbacks` across a reconnect, but `resubscribe` sends only one
SUBSCRIBE per channel in `@subscribers`. This misfires in two cases:

1. **Removed and re-added during the outage.** The channel ends up with two
   pending callbacks (`[cb1, cb2]`); the single resubscribe acknowledgement
   shifts and runs only `cb1`, and `cb2` waits for an acknowledgement that
   never comes — the re-added subscription is never confirmed.
2. **Removed before the reconnect.** The stale `cb1` is kept even though
   `resubscribe` skips the channel; the next `add_subscriber` queues `cb2`
   behind it, and that subscribe's one acknowledgement runs the stale `cb1`
   while the new subscription is never confirmed.

The fix, in `Listener#reset`:

- Drop confirmations for channels that no longer have subscribers
  (`@subscribe_callbacks.select! { |channel, _| @subscribers.key?(channel) }`),
  so they cannot consume a later subscribe's acknowledgement.
- Merge each remaining channel's pending confirmations into a single flat
  entry (`transform_values! { |callbacks| [callbacks.flatten.compact] }`),
  and run the whole entry on one acknowledgement
  (`Array(callbacks.shift).each { |callback| @executor.post(&callback) }`).
  `flatten` is idempotent, so any number of failed reconnects leaves the
  entry flat.

The lock order (`@sync`, then `@subscription_lock`) matches
`add_subscriber` -> `add_channel`. In case 1 the merged entry also runs the
removed subscriber's stale `cb1`; confirmation callbacks are fire-and-forget
notifications, so running a stale one is harmless — what matters is that the
live subscription's confirmation is no longer starved.

This Pull Request changes `PostgreSQL::SchemaDumper#schemas` to also dump the schemas that dumped extensions are qualified with, when `dump_schemas` leaves them out:


- `if_not_exists: true` keeps the dump loadable where the platform creates the schema already (Supabase's `extensions` or `graphql`). That was the reason #58834 ruled out a plain `create_schema`.

- `public` and `pg_*` schemas are skipped: they always exist, and PostgreSQL rejects `CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS pg_catalog` ("The prefix "pg_" is reserved for system schemas").

**Description**

`composer run setup` bootstraps an environment, but it is only mostly safe to run more than once. Every step converges to the same end state on a repeat run, except `key:generate`:

- `composer install` installs exactly what `composer.lock` specifies.
- The `.env` copy is guarded with `file_exists('.env') ||`.
- `migrate --force` only applies pending migrations.
- `npm install` and `npm run build` are deterministic for a given lockfile and source tree.
- `artisan key:generate` generates a new `APP_KEY` on every invocation.

Outside production, `key:generate` does not check for an existing key. It only calls `confirmToProceed()`, which auto-confirms, so it silently overwrites the key (see `KeyGenerateCommand::setKeyInEnvironmentFile()`). In production it prompts, which fails under `--no-interaction`.

**Why this matters**

Re-running setup rotates the encryption key. Active sessions are invalidated, signed URLs stop validating, and anything encrypted can no longer be decrypted. Because the other steps are safe to repeat, setup looks like a routine "setup my environment" command while hiding one destructive side effect.

**Reproduce**

```sh
composer run setup
grep ^APP_KEY= .env   # APP_KEY=base64:AAAA...

composer run setup
grep ^APP_KEY= .env   # APP_KEY=base64:BBBB...  <- key changed
```

**Change**

`key:generate` only runs when `.env` has no `APP_KEY` or an empty one:

```diff
-    "@php artisan key:generate",
+    "@php -r \"if (!preg_match('/^APP_KEY=.+/m', file_get_contents('.env'))) { passthru(PHP_BINARY.' artisan key:generate --ansi', \\$c); exit(\\$c); }\"",
```

- A plain `@php artisan key:generate` cannot be made conditional: composer scripts have no conditionals, and `@php` is only expanded at the start of a command. The guard therefore uses the same `@php -r` style as the existing `.env` copy step.
- `PHP_BINARY` runs artisan with the same PHP that composer uses.
- `passthru()` streams artisan's output (including ANSI colors) straight to the terminal.
- The exit code is passed on with `exit($c)`, so a failing `key:generate` still fails the script. `$c` is escaped (`\\$c`) because composer runs the line through a shell that would otherwise expand it.

**Result**

`composer run setup` can be run any number of times and converges to the same state, keeping the existing key. Destructive resets stay explicit and separate.

**Testing**

```sh
composer run setup
grep ^APP_KEY= .env   # APP_KEY=base64:AAAA...

composer run setup
grep ^APP_KEY= .env   # APP_KEY=base64:AAAA...  <- key not changed
```

**Scope note**

The guard only inspects `.env`. If `APP_KEY` comes purely from a real environment variable, `.env` may still get a generated key. That is harmless, since real environment variables take precedence over `.env` in Laravel.

`simd` and `simdarch` (arm64 and amd64) implementations of hex encode/decode

----

Implementation details 

On amd64 Encode widens each byte 0xHL to the uint16 0x00HL and
multiplies it by 0x1001, which gives 0xL0HL; shifted right by 4 it is
0x0L0H, the two nibbles in output order, and one VPSHUFB turns them into
digits. Decode computes the nibbles and checks the characters in one
pass, by algorithm 3 of
http://0x80.pl/notesen/2022-01-17-validating-hex-parse.html, and packs
them with VPMADDUBSW and VPSHUFB.

On arm64 Encode looks up both nibbles with TBL and interleaves the
digits with ZIP1 and ZIP2. Decode computes the nibbles as on amd64 and
packs them with UZP1 and UZP2.

----

The portable kernels are slower because every 64-bit lane works alone
and scalar stores join the lanes. What portable `simd` package lacks:

- interleaving the bytes of two vectors, or zero-extending half of a
  Uint8s to Uint16s (VPUNPCKLBW or VPMOVZXBW; ZIP1 or UXTL), for Encode
- narrowing Uint16s to Uint8s, or taking the even bytes of two vectors
  (VPACKUSWB; UZP1 or XTN), for Decode
- a byte table lookup (VPSHUFB; TBL), which saves a few operations in
  Encode
- comparisons and shifts on Uint8s, which only Int8s and wider types
  have
- clearing the upper bits of the AVX registers before returning:
  archsimd.ClearAVXUpperBits has no portable counterpart, and the
  compiler does not insert VZEROUPPER (#80835)

## Summary
Minor performance optimizations in `requests/auth.py`, specifically in
`HTTPDigestAuth`. No behavioral or API changes — outputs are byte-for-byte
identical to before for all inputs.

## Changes

1. **Hoist digest hash-function closures to module scope**
   `build_digest_header()` previously defined four nested closures
   (`md5_utf8`, `sha_utf8`, `sha256_utf8`, `sha512_utf8`) on *every* call,
   i.e. on every digest-authenticated request. These are now module-level
   functions (`_md5_utf8`, etc.) selected once via a precomputed
   `_DIGEST_HASH_FUNCS` dict, replacing the if/elif chain with a single
   dict lookup.

2. **Compile the digest-scheme regex once**
   `handle_401()` recompiled `re.compile(r"digest ", flags=re.IGNORECASE)`
   on every 401 response. It's now a module-level constant
   (`_DIGEST_SCHEME_RE`) compiled once at import time.

3. **Single `bytes.join()` instead of repeated `+=`**
   The cnonce seed in `build_digest_header()` was built via four
   successive `+=` concatenations on a `bytes` object, each allocating a
   new object. Replaced with a single `b"".join(...)`.

## Why this is safe
- All three changes are pure refactors of *how* the same values are
  computed, not *what* is computed. Function bodies, algorithm selection
  logic, and string/byte outputs are unchanged.
- Existing test suite passes unmodified.

## Testing
- Ran the full `auth` test suite (`pytest tests/test_requests.py -k auth`) — all passing.
- Isolated microbenchmark (`timeit`, N=200,000) comparing old vs new
  implementations of the changed code paths:

  | Change                                   | Old (us/call) | New (us/call) | Speedup |
  |-------------------------------------------|---------------|----------------|---------|
  | Hash-function selection (closures → dict) | 0.167         | 0.071          | 2.3x    |
  | Regex stripping (compile → precompiled)   | 0.824         | 0.393          | 2.1x    |
  | cnonce seed (chained += → join)           | 2.180         | 1.952          | 1.1x    |

  These are microbenchmarks on the isolated logic, not end-to-end request
  timings — real-world impact is dominated by network I/O, but this removes
  unnecessary per-call allocation/compilation overhead on the digest-auth
  hot path, which matters under high request volume.

When `trust proxy` is a subnet list (e.g. `loopback, 10.0.0.0/8`), the trust check on the socket address is slow (~1us), and `req.protocol`, `req.host` and `req.hostname` each repeat it. `req.ip` runs `proxy-addr` on every access (~2us). Middleware like logging or rate limiting often reads these more than once per request.

This keeps the result on the request and reuses it while its inputs are the same:

- the trust check for the socket address is shared by `protocol`, `secure`, `host`, `hostname` and `subdomains` (key: trust function and socket address)
- `req.ip` (key: trust function, socket address and `X-Forwarded-For`)

If any of those change, it is computed again, so the returned values are the same as before. `req.ips` is not changed because it returns an array.

Micro benchmark per access with `trust proxy` set to `loopback, 10.0.0.0/8`:

- `req.ip`: ~2150ns -> ~64ns
- `req.protocol`: ~1080ns -> ~140ns
- `req.host`: ~1110ns -> ~100ns

With `trust proxy` off or `true` these were already cheap (10-250ns), so there is not much difference there.

The next-generation trait solver is the product of 4 years of active work by multiple people and is based on what we've learned from working on Chalk for years before then.

It is the largest single change to Rust since version 1.0. It has has a significant impact on the behavior of the type system in edge-cases, its performance, and our mental model of it. However, its main benefits will come down the road as we stabilize features and improvements which are only possible thanks to it. The most immediate impact will likely be the stabilization of [TAIT/RTN](https://goals.rust-lang.org/2026/rtn.html), which was blocked on our rework of opaque types.

This report does not go into the history of the solver and also does not properly appreciate all the people involved. Getting to this point would not have been possible by myself and I want to spend the time to properly document all the effort that went into it as part of an announcement blog post before this reaches stable. Even so, I want to already thank @compiler-errors and @adwinwhite here. They have both done incredibly good work on the new trait solver and without their contributions this stabilization would probably not have been possible at all.

See https://github.com/rust-lang/goals/issues/113 for an overview of all the work that went into the trait solver since late 2024. Also see the [blog post announcing it on nightly](https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/08/21/enabling-next-solver-on-nightly). The Rust tracking issue is https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/107374.

## Technical overview

Given the size of this stabilization, the actual technical documentation and overview is in the [Trait System Refactor Initiative repository](https://github.com/rust-lang/trait-system-refactor-initiative/blob/main/notes/stabilization-report/meta.md). If you have any questions, please reach out on [zulip](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/channel/364551-t-types.2Ftrait-system-refactor/topic/casual.20chat.20and.20support/with/628633853). We will continuously update this overview as we move forward.

## How will this stabilization work

Stabilizing the new trait solver is an incredibly large change which also has a huge impact on diagnostics. This makes updating the UI test suite quite challenging. I've spent the last few weeks going through all tests which change their result. See https://hackmd.io/ydc_nIbHQqG-ctMDapXYTg for an overview the impact on non-UI test suites.

See https://github.com/lcnr/rust/pull/12 for the remaining changes when running our UI test suite with the new solver. There are a lot of diagnostics regressions here and also far too many changes to review in a single PR. We currently enable the new solver on nightly by default while explicitly disabling the next-solver in all test suites affected by it.

**Stabilizing the new solver will cause us to also use it on `beta` and then `stable` starting in version 1.101. The beta cutoff is on November 6th. We will initially keep forcefully using the old solver in our test suites.**

Then, over the next weeks, we incrementally update all test suites to use the new solver. Doing this incrementally allows us to actually review and address the changes and make sure that diagnostics issues are caught and addressed. We will also finish triaging all crater regressions and open PRs or at least issues to all affected crates we are aware of.

After the next beta-cutoff, and once we've updated all test suites to no longer rely on `-Znext-solver=coherence`, we will remove the old solver. **This means we are only able to delay the stabilization by at most one release if necessary.** Reverting the stabilization at all has a high cost. It exposes the fact that the old trait solver has not been tested on nightly since we've enabled the new one in August.

## My personal thoughts here

I would have really liked the new trait solver to be perfect pre-stabilization. It's clear that waiting until literally all issues have been fixed is not tenable. I have been thinking a lot about whether delaying it by one more release would be better.

Right now there are still some hangs, performance is on average worse, there are quite a few poor diagnostics and minor remaining bugs. Spending 6 more weeks to improve the new solver would make all of this less of an issue, given the amount of active work currently going on.

After some private discussions I think stabilizing this in 1.101 is still preferable due to the following reasons:
- we're blocking a bunch of work on the new trait solver being stable, either because we're not testing the old solver right now, or because the change is hard to implement with the old solver
- having two trait solvers in the compiler results in an incredible amount of complexity, is confusing to other contributors, and negatively impacts performance
- the current state of the new solver being enabled on nightly while not being stable is confusing and causes issues, it results in both implementions not getting the test coverage they should ideally have
- having the new solver means we do a lot of changes without Types Team FCPs which should really be FCP'd by the wider team. The new trait solver is too large to appropriately review all its changes. Once the new solver is stable, we can incrementally improve it going forward.
- keeping the old solver enabled by default results in new crates depending on intentionally broken behavior, e.g. `tera-2.0.0` was recently published while depending on https://github.com/rust-lang/trait-system-refactor-initiative/issues/168. The unintended breakage from stabilizing the new solver is less impactful than the unintended incorrect behavior of the old solver
- breaking less than 500 crates on crater, with nearly all of this being intended breakage of a few root crates, is definitely fine. Even considering the performance issues which are hard to uncover via crater, this still feels very acceptable to me

### Motivation / Background

This Pull Request has been created because the Action Cable Redis adapter's connection pool can't be configured, and its defaults are tight enough to fail broadcasts under load.

- **Where the pool comes from:** since the adapter moved to redis-client in #57533, broadcasts go through `RedisClient.config(...).new_pool` with no arguments. That gives redis-client's defaults: 5 connections and a 1 second checkout timeout.
- **What happens under load:** with 5 threads already publishing, a sixth that can't get a connection within a second raises `RedisClient::CheckoutTimeoutError` from `ActionCable.server.broadcast`. We hit this in a Sidekiq process with 25 threads streaming log output through Turbo Stream broadcasts: `Couldn't checkout a connection in time: Waited 1.0 sec, 0/5 available`. Before #57533, broadcasts shared one `Redis` connection and waited their turn instead.
- **Why it can't be configured today:** every key in `cable.yml` except `adapter` and `channel_prefix` goes to `RedisClient.config`, which rejects `pool` with `ArgumentError: unknown keyword: :pool`. The only way to change the pool is replacing `redis_connector`.

### Detail

This Pull Request changes the default `redis_connector` to pass a `pool` hash from the config to `new_pool`, the same option `RedisCacheStore` takes:

```yaml
production:
  adapter: redis
  url: <%= ENV["REDIS_URL"] %>
  pool:
    size: 10
    timeout: 5
```

Without `pool`, nothing changes: the pool keeps redis-client's defaults.

### Additional information

The 1 second default checkout timeout comes from redis-client (`RedisClient::Config::DEFAULT_TIMEOUT`). `RedisCacheStore` defaults to `{ size: 5, timeout: 5 }`, and `ConnectionPool`'s own default timeout is also 5. Matching that here might be a better default, but I've kept this PR to making the pool configurable. Happy to change the default here or in a follow-up if that's preferred.

`app.listen(cb)` registers `cb` as a one-off `'error'` listener so that errors
raised while binding (such as `EADDRINUSE`) are delivered to the callback, but
that listener is never removed. After a successful start the server still
carries it, and since it has already been called it does nothing — it consumes
the first later `'error'` event instead of letting it keep the normal
`EventEmitter` semantics.

Remove the listener from the `'listening'` event, which fires before the user
callback runs. Errors raised while binding are emitted before `'listening'`, so
they still reach the callback.

The new tests assert that no `'error'` listener is left behind and that a later
`emit('error')` is no longer swallowed.

This replaces `hydratable` with `Warp`, a `Map` whose contents get sent from the server to the client. It's built on devalue's new `unevalStream`, which sets up streaming SSR in the next PR in this stack. On its own, this PR shouldn't change behavior much: the server still waits for every promise before responding, just like `hydratable` does today.

```js
import { Warp } from 'svelte';

const warp = new Warp('my-lib');
const user = await warp.getOrInsertComputed('user', () => getUser());
```

Each `Warp` has an id, so libraries don't collide with each other. `hydratable` is now just an internal `Warp`, and is deprecated. It's deprecated in JSDoc only, with no runtime warning: a warn-once-per-process message would make tests pass or fail depending on the order they run in. On the client, `Warp` behaves like a real `Map` (`set`, `delete` and friends all work), so it doubles as a cache. On the server, each key can only be set once, and `delete` and `clear` throw. Something may already have read the value during the render, or it may already be on its way to the client, so replacing it would mean the client hydrates with different data than the server rendered with. `getOrInsert(Computed)` is unaffected, and uses the native `Map` method when there is one.

There's also `withWarp` in `svelte/server`, for adding values before a render starts (in load functions, for example). A `render` inside it uses its context, and only one `render` is allowed per `withWarp`. Both `withWarp` and `render` take a devalue `replacer`. When both are given, the render's replacer runs first.

How the serialization works: the whole store goes through a single `unevalStream` call, and we read the tail to the end immediately and append it to the head script. Promises that have already settled are resolved in that same `<script>` before hydration runs, so the output is still a single `<script>`, as before, and devalue handles nested promises itself.

- Rejected promises now reject on the client, after passing through `render`'s `transformError`, and the client's `failed` boundary can handle them. Previously a rejection failed the whole render.
- Values that can't be serialized still fail the render, with `warp_serialization_failed`. If the problem is in the head, `unevalStream` throws. If it's in a resolved value, devalue passes a `DevalueError` to `transformError`, which we catch and rethrow once the tail is done. The error includes devalue's path to the bad value.
- `unresolved_hydratable` is now `unresolved_warp`, and is less precise. It fires if the tail isn't done within a macrotask of the render finishing, but it can't say which key is responsible, because devalue doesn't know. Since `unresolved_warp` is basically temporary, that seemed fine.

Tests: `warp.test.ts` covers the server API, `withWarp`, replacers, rejections and escaping. The runtime samples from the old `elliott/warp` branch are ported, plus a new `warp-rejected` sample where a server rejection ends up in a client `failed` snippet.

One thing to sort out before merging: devalue's `types.d.ts` uses `AsyncIterableIterator<string, void>`, which needs TS 5.6, so `pnpm check` fails on our 5.5.4 unless you pass `--skipLibCheck`. This should probably be fixed in devalue rather than here. It's on the prerelease build anyway, until devalue ships `unevalStream`.

## Summary

- Add `isHandlingError` guard to prevent infinite recursion when the custom error handler itself throws an error
- Previously, if `config.errorHandler` threw, it would trigger `handleError` again, which calls the error handler again, causing infinite recursion and `Maximum call stack size exceeded`
- The guard ensures that if `handleError` is called while already handling an error, it returns early instead of re-entering the error handling flow

## Problem

When a custom `config.errorHandler` throws an error, the following chain occurs:
1. `invokeWithErrorHandling` catches the original error
2. Calls `handleError`
3. `handleError` calls `globalHandleError`
4. `globalHandleError` calls `config.errorHandler`
5. If `errorHandler` throws, it calls `logError`
6. If `logError` or any code path leads back to `invokeWithErrorHandling`, the cycle repeats
7. Result: `RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded`

## Changes

- Added module-level `isHandlingError` flag
- Set flag to `true` at the start of `handleError`
- Early return with `popTarget()` if already handling an error
- Reset flag to `false` in the `finally` block
- Added test case to verify the fix

processURLOnto implements the URL escaper and normalizer, used for
actions in URL attributes such as href and src, and the srcset
filter. It had three costs unrelated to escaping itself:

- It wrote each percent-encoded byte with fmt.Fprintf(b, "%%%02x", c),
  which is an expensive operation, consuming 56% of CPU time in the
  URL escaping benchmarks on linux/amd64.
- Passing b to Fprintf as an io.Writer made every caller's
  strings.Builder escape to the heap.
- Eager memory allocation before looking at the input.

Escaping a URL that needs no changes made 2 allocations (96 B).

Write the escape bytes directly. Grow b only when the first byte that
needs escaping is found, and append nothing when the URL is unchanged.
filterSrcsetElement, which needs the URL appended either way, now
writes unchanged URLs itself. It grows b by len(url)+16 before each
URL as processURLOnto did before, to keep the growth policy introduced
for #24731. The output is unchanged.

### Motivation / Background

SQLite rolls back the transaction itself when a statement or `COMMIT` fails with errors such as `SQLITE_FULL`, `SQLITE_IOERR` or `SQLITE_NOMEM`. The SQLite3 adapter then still runs `ROLLBACK`, which fails with `cannot rollback - no transaction is active`. That second exception:

- replaces the original error. The caller gets `StatementInvalid: cannot rollback - no transaction is active`, and the real `SQLite3::FullException` is two levels down in `#cause`, so `rescue` and retry logic keyed on the real error never matches;
- escapes before `rollback_records` runs. Records created in the transaction stay `persisted?` and keep their `id` for rows that do not exist, and `after_rollback` callbacks do not fire.

Reproduced on `main` with stock SQLite (3.53.2, sqlite3 2.9.6). `PRAGMA max_page_count` makes the transaction run out of pages:

```ruby
Item.transaction do
  first = Item.create!(body: "x")
  50.times { Item.create!(body: "y" * 20_000) }
end
```

```
# before
ActiveRecord::StatementInvalid: SQLite3::SQLException: cannot rollback - no transaction is active
  <- ... <- SQLite3::FullException: database or disk is full
first.persisted? # => true, first.id # => 1, rows in table: 0, after_rollback calls: 0

# after
ActiveRecord::StatementInvalid: SQLite3::FullException: database or disk is full
first.persisted? # => false, first.id # => nil, after_rollback calls: 1
```

A real full disk does the same thing: a database on a 2 MB tmpfs whose `COMMIT` hits `SQLITE_FULL` gives the same output.

### Detail

`SQLite3Adapter#exec_rollback_db_transaction` now returns early when the raw connection reports no open transaction (`SQLite3::Database#transaction_active?`, which is `!sqlite3_get_autocommit`). The rest of the rollback path, including `rollback_records`, runs as before.

### Additional information

- Added `SQLite3AutoRollbackTest`. It fails without the change (`Expected #<SQLite3::SQLException: cannot rollback - no transaction is active> to be an instance of SQLite3::FullException`) and passes with it.
- `rake test:sqlite3` with the change: 9,890 runs, 0 failures. There is 1 error, `ConnectionHandlersMultiDbTest#test_switching_connections_with_database_url`, because `pg` isn't installed on my machine. It errors the same way without the change.

### Motivation / Background

`NumberToRoundedConverter#format_number` builds two regexps from the separator on every call when `strip_insignificant_zeros` is on. That is the default for `number_to_human_size` and `number_to_human`, and it is also used by `number_to_rounded(strip_insignificant_zeros: true)`.

The separator is almost always `"."` or `","`, so compiling the same regexps again on every call is wasted work.

### Detail

This Pull Request builds the regexps for `"."` and `","` once, in a frozen constant. Any other separator still builds them per call, like today. I kept it to those two on purpose: the constant can't grow, and it stays Ractor shareable.

Allocations per call:

| Call | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| `number_to_human_size(1234567)` | 148 | 132 |
| `number_to_human(1234567)` | 178 | 162 |
| `number_to_rounded(12.34, precision: 4, strip_insignificant_zeros: true)` | 81 | 65 |

Speed (both versions in the same process, run alternately 30-40 times, best time of each):

| Call | No YJIT | YJIT |
|---|---|---|
| `number_to_human_size(1234567)` | +10% | +18% |
| `number_to_human(1234567)` | +8% | +13% |
| `number_to_rounded(..., strip_insignificant_zeros: true)` | +21% | +39% |
| same, with `separator: "\|"` (uncached path) | -0.8% | +0.4% |

Rollup merge of #163425 - ojuschugh1:jump-threading-fix, r=saethlin

Treat union fields as aliasing each other in value_analysis

Fixes rust-lang/rust#161898

The problem was that `for_each_aliasing_place` only considered enum variants and the discriminant as aliasing, so writing to one union field left the state of the other fields alone. JumpThreading then threaded the second `switchInt` on `u.a` using the value from before `u.b = 5`, and DataflowConstProp folded the read of `u.a` to a stale constant in the same way. Union field places have only been in the map since rust-lang/rust#127087 began collecting places syntactically; before that `iter_fields` skipped unions.

I made `for_each_aliasing_place` flood everything under a union as soon as the walk reaches it, since all non-ZST union fields start at offset 0 and overlap. The alternative of not registering places below unions would also work but loses threading on union reads with no write in between.

Adds a path-containment check to `View.prototype.lookup()` so a resolved view path must stay inside the configured views directory, mirroring the root containment `res.sendFile()` gets from the `send` library.

After resolving, the resolved path is checked against `resolve(root) + path.sep`; views outside the root are skipped by the existing iteration.

Fixes the remaining cases of the incorrect expansion fixed in CL 685755
(#74466).

On Windows, names whose final path element consists only of dots — "abc/..",
"abc/.", "./", ... — are not rejected by validateLookPath, and the extension
probing in findExecutable/lookPathExts concatenates a PATHEXT extension onto
the dots element, resolving a different file: "abc/.." resolves "abc/...exe"
(nil error), "abc/." resolves "abc/..exe", and "./" resolves "./.exe".
Cmd.Start then executes that file. The OS's own resolution never resolves
these names.

This extends the fix from CL 685755: validateLookPath now rejects any name
whose final element, ignoring trailing path separators, consists only of
dots. The check is in the shared (platform-independent) code path, so
behavior is consistent across platforms.

Testing:
- Added subtests to dot_test.go ("dots-only elements", "dots-only in PATH
  dir"): they plant the files that extension probing would wrongly resolve
  and assert LookPath errors. On Windows these fail without the fix.
- go test os/exec passes on the patched tree (linux).
- Additionally exercised with windows/amd64 builds of a probe: every
  dots-only form stops resolving, existing behaviors are preserved ("abc/"
  still resolves "abc/.exe" as the OS does; cwd-relative ErrDot cases
  unchanged).

Speed up String#blank? with a byte loop for ASCII-only strings

String#blank? matched every string against /\A[[:space:]]*\z/. Most
strings an application checks are ASCII, and for those a few byte
comparisons settle the question: a printable first character means the
string is not blank, otherwise a loop over the bytes accepts only space,
\t, \n, \v, \f and \r. Under YJIT the loop allocates nothing and is
several times faster than entering the regexp engine.

Strings containing non-ASCII characters keep using the regexp, which
knows the Unicode whitespace codepoints and each legacy encoding's
whitespace table. They pay one ascii_only? call before reaching it. The
empty string is unchanged.

Parity with the regexp was checked on every single character of all 94
non-dummy encodings and on fuzzed multi-character strings.

This Pull Request has been created because a nested `pin_connection!(true)` replaces the lock an outer pin installed. TestProf's `before_all` followed by transactional fixtures nests two such pins for every test, so a thread already inside the old lock (in our case, most likely a system test's app server finishing a request) shares the raw connection with the test's next statement. On PostgreSQL that surfaces as `NoMethodError: undefined method 'cmd_tuples' for nil`, `PG::UnableToSend`, or a hang.

### Detail

This Pull Request changes `ConnectionPool#pin_connection!` to install a lock only when the connection has none, so a nested pin leaves the existing one in place. `unpin_connection!` already resets the lock only once the last pin is released.

The nesting tests added in #52037 cover `pin(true)` then `pin(false)`, and the reverse. The new `test_pin_connection_nesting_keeps_lock` covers `pin(true)` twice; it fails on `main` under both thread and fiber isolation, and passes with this change.

### Additional information

The issue has a standalone reproduction in which a statement on the re-pinned connection runs while another thread still holds the original lock.

Related, but separate: #58478 and #58490 concern `checkout` across an unpin and a re-pin to a different connection.

Based on [this concern](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/106418#issuecomment-1994833151) on the implementation of `Partial/Ord` for `Discriminant`, I'm proposing we instead offer an `unstable_cmp` function. This mirrors the `fN::total_cmp` function used to provide `Ord`-like functionality to `f16/32/64/128` without actually guaranteeing the type itself is `Ord`.

# Notes

* No AI tooling of any kind was used during the creation of this PR.
* The name `unstable_cmp` has been chosen to explicitly document at each usage that the ordering of `Discriminant` values is *not* stable and *may* change.

Codegen emits `debugger;` without a source location, so Babel's source map attributes it to the end of the preceding statement. ## Description

When a client disconnects mid-stream, the WSGI server abandons the body
iterator. The generator is later finalized by the garbage collector, often
on a **different thread** than the one that pushed the context.

`ctx.pop()` raises `RuntimeError` because `_cv_app.get(None)` returns `None`
on the GC thread. The context stays "stuck" on the original worker thread,
and `teardown_appcontext` never fires for subsequent requests on that thread.

## Fix

Replace `with ctx:` with manual `ctx.push()` / `ctx.pop()` in the
`stream_with_context` generator. Wrap `pop()` in a try/except that catches
`RuntimeError` and resets the context state (`_push_count` and `_cv_token`)
to prevent thread pool poisoning.

Linux time64 syscalls use `__kernel_timespec`, with signed 64-bit seconds and nanoseconds. The MIPS runtime currently uses an `int32` nanoseconds field followed by padding. On big-endian MIPS this puts nanoseconds in the upper half of the syscall field, causing subsecond futex waits and profiling intervals to be interpreted as zero.

- Replace `console.warn` calls with Vue's `warn()` function in the hydration mismatch code paths
- Hydration warnings now respect `config.warnHandler` instead of always going to `console.warn`

## Problem

During SSR hydration, when the client-side virtual DOM doesn't match the server-rendered HTML, Vue logs warnings using `console.warn` directly. This has two issues:

1. These warnings are not routed through `config.warnHandler`, so production apps with a custom warn handler can't capture them
2. The `console.warn` calls are guarded by `__DEV__` and `typeof console !== 'undefined'`, meaning they're completely stripped in production — but a configured `warnHandler` should still be able to receive them in dev mode
3. The warnings don't include the element tag name, making it harder to identify which element has the mismatch

## Changes

- Replaced `console.warn('Parent: ', elm)` + `console.warn('server innerHTML: ', i)` + `console.warn('client innerHTML: ', elm.innerHTML)` with a single structured `warn()` call that includes the tag name and both server/client values
- Replaced `console.warn('Parent: ', elm)` + `console.warn('Mismatching childNodes vs. VNodes: ', ...)` with a single `warn()` call that includes the tag name and child node counts
- Removed the `typeof console !== 'undefined'` guards since `warn()` handles this internally

[DOM] Stop emulating bubbling for toggle and beforetoggle events (#37580)

## Summary

Fixes #22718.

**Root cause:** `toggle` and `beforetoggle` (fired by `<details>`,
`<dialog>`, and the Popover API) don't bubble natively in the DOM, and
they were already listed in `nonDelegatedEvents` (native listener
attached directly to the target). However, `SimpleEventPlugin`'s
`accumulateTargetOnly` check — which controls whether React accumulates
listeners for just the target vs. the whole ancestor chain — only
special-cased `scroll`/`scrollend`. So `toggle`/`beforetoggle` still had
their listeners accumulated up the fiber tree, meaning ancestor
`onToggle`/`onBeforeToggle` handlers could fire even though the native
event never reached them.

**Fix:** Extend the existing `accumulateTargetOnly` condition in
`packages/react-dom-bindings/src/events/plugins/SimpleEventPlugin.js` to
also cover `toggle` and `beforetoggle`, aligning them with the
scroll/scrollend non-bubbling precedent. No other files touched.

**Tests:** Moved the existing `onToggle`/`onBeforeToggle` test cases
(plain `<details>`, Popover API, Dialog API) in
`ReactDOMEventPropagation-test.js` from the "non-bubbling events that
bubble in React" describe block (`testEmulatedBubblingEvent`) into
"non-bubbling events that do not bubble in React"
(`testNonBubblingEvent`), matching how `onScroll`/`onScrollEnd` are
tested. Also added a small `...eventConfig.targetProps` spread to the
`testNonBubblingEvent*` helpers so `targetProps` (e.g. `popover: 'any'`)
reach the fixture, mirroring the `testEmulatedBubblingEvent*` helpers.

In _panic.nextFrame, searching for the frame containing linked defers
(limit = gp._defer.sp) only compared u.frame.sp == limit. On
architectures where leaf calls do not adjust the stack pointer or in
the presence of frameless leaf wrappers, a callee wrapper shares the
exact same SP as its caller. When panicking inside such a wrapper,
nextFrame prematurely broke on the wrapper frame. Because the frameless
wrapper has no saved link register on the stack, subsequent traceback
initialization from p.pc failed with "fatal error: traceback did not
unwind completely".

Require u.frame.fn == findfunc(d.pc) in addition to u.frame.sp == limit
before stopping at a frame with linked defers. This ensures nextFrame
skips frameless wrappers and unwinds to the actual function that
registered the defer.

Add ADDQcarryload, ADCQload, SUBQborrowload and SBBQload, which read the second operand of a carry or borrow chain link from memory, and merge a MOVQload into ADDQcarry, ADCQ, SUBQborrow and SBBQ when possible. For

	_, c := bits.Add64(a[0], b[0], 0)
	_, c2 := bits.Add64(a[1], b[1], c)

the compiler now emits

	ADDQ	a(SP), DX
	ADCQ	b+24(SP), BX

instead of loading each operand into a register first.

The new ops also absorb FlagEQ and InvertFlags carry inputs, as ADCQ and SBBQ do (see #79887), and fold constant offsets and LEAQ into their address.

flagalloc restores a flag value by copying its generator and, through copyFlags, the generators of that generator's flag inputs: the earlier links of a carry chain. A copy runs later than the original, possibly after a store, so it must not read memory. flagalloc only split generators that were themselves spilled; it now splits, before copying anything, every generator that may be copied and reads memory. Without this, a carry that must survive a call made the compiler fail with "can't move a value with a memory arg". On std and cmd the set of values that flagalloc splits is unchanged.

When both the result and the carry of a link are used, lowering builds two identical ADCQ values that are only merged by the lowered CSE pass, after the load merging rules have run, so such links still load their operand into a register. That leaves the middle links of multi-word additions unchanged; fixing it needs a change to how Add64carry and Sub64borrow are lowered.

Fixes #82001.

Since CL 222619 (Go 1.15), the C wrapper that cgo writes to
_cgo_export.c for an exported function uses the Go parameter names
as the C parameter names. The wrapper body declares a struct whose
fields use the C types of the parameters and results, so a parameter
whose name is the same as a C type name shadows that type and the
wrapper fails to compile:

	//export F
	func F(writeFunc C.writeFunc) { ... }

	_cgo_export.c: error: expected specifier-qualifier-list
	before 'writeFunc'

Similarly, a parameter named r conflicts with the local variable
that holds multiple results.

Keep the Go parameter names in the declaration in _cgo_export.h,
which is what CL 222619 was for, but use the generated names p0, p1,
... in the definition, as was done before Go 1.15. C does not
require the parameter names of a declaration and a definition to
match, so the header seen by users is unchanged.

Stacked on #18963.

Right now, when SSR reaches a `<svelte:boundary>` with a `pending` snippet, it renders the snippet and skips everything inside the boundary. The client then renders the boundary's contents itself, which means any data they need only starts loading after hydration. That's a waterfall that wouldn't happen if the server had just started the work.

With the new `experimental.streaming` compiler option, the server renders the pending snippet and also runs the boundary's children in the background, throwing away their HTML. Any `Warp` values the children create get streamed to the client, which waits for those instead of fetching them again.

```js
const { head, body, tail } = await render(App);

res.write(`<html><head>${head}</head><body>${body}`);
for await (const script of tail) res.write(script);
res.end('</body></html>');
```

How it works:

- **Compiler:** the server output for a pending boundary now emits `$$renderer.background(children)` after the pending snippet. Without the option, the output is the same as before.
- **No global runtime flag:** a render streams only when it actually has background work. The `tail` is always there, but it's empty otherwise. I tried a global flag first, but it leaks across every component in the process, and across every test in the runtime suite too.
- **Separate state for background work:** it gets its own `SSRState`, so it can't affect the title, CSS or ids of the real HTML. It's aborted, and its `onDestroy` callbacks run, once it settles or once the consumer stops reading the `tail`. The webcontainer render lock is held until it's done.
- **Splitting head and tail:** it's the same single `unevalStream` call as in #18963. The difference is that instead of reading the tail to the end, we only take the blocks that are ready now, i.e. the ones that arrive before a macrotask. Promises that had already settled resolve within microtasks, so those blocks go into the head script. Anything awaited outside a pending boundary is settled by then, so there's no need to track which `await`s happen where. Everything else becomes `tail`.
- **Values set after the head is generated:** a background component will often `await` one value and then create another (`posts:${user.id}`). Those values go out through a chain of promises in the payload, where each one resolves to a batch of new values plus the next promise. A replacer turns each batch into code that writes into `window.__svelte.w` *as the tail script runs*. So if the batch arrives in the same chunk as the promise it depends on, the values are already in place before the client continues.
- **Batching chunks:** the tail's blocks are combined per macrotask before being wrapped in `<script nonce>`. This gives server work that was waiting on a promise that just resolved time to add its own values to the same chunk. If something still arrives late, the client falls back to computing it, the same as today.
- **Client changes while streaming:** if the client changed `window.__svelte.w` directly while values were streaming in, a late value could undo a `delete` or `clear`, depending on timing. So while a stream is in progress, `set`/`delete`/`clear` on the client go into an overlay instead. It's just a `cleared` flag plus a map of changes and tombstones, and it keeps the same key order a `Map` would. Reads go through the overlay, and it's applied to the real values the next time the `Warp` is used after the stream finishes. The head script increments `window.__svelte.s` and the last tail script decrements it. "Streaming" means `s > 0` *and* `document.readyState === 'loading'`, so a dropped connection can't leave it stuck. Client changes win over values from the server, including ones that arrive later, so a pending component whose data was cleared just loads it again on the client.
- `csp.hash` combined with streaming throws `invalid_csp_streaming`, since we can't hash scripts that haven't been produced yet.

`hydratable` doesn't get any of this, since it only reads server data while hydrating. Think of it as a carrot for migrating to `Warp`.

The big caveat: if you turn this on and don't write out `tail`, client promises never settle. That's why it's an experimental flag aimed at frameworks rather than something on by default. The docs say so in bold.

Tests: unit tests in `warp.test.ts` cover inlining, streaming, late values, same-chunk ordering, aborting when the tail is abandoned, CSP, and output being discarded. There are runtime samples (`streaming-warp`, `streaming-warp-nested`, `streaming-warp-rejected`) where hydration shows the server's data instead of recomputing it. There's also a compiler snapshot.

endpoint through the aggregation mapping before forwarding the condition. The SQL is
still built by the existing code path. Covers exclusive, beginless/endless ranges, and
ranges nested in an array. Composite aggregations are not handled in this PR and remains unchanged.
